title: Cost & staging pilot intake - Ventana Corp
next_steps: Redwood: send per-token pricing + pilot SOW by 2025-10-01
Ventana: share sample workload (1 week) and auth IP allowlist for benchmark
action_items: Alex Moreno - send model pricing matrix & committed capacity pricing (Due: 2025-10-01)
Samira Patel - propose benchmark test plan and metrics (Due: 2025-09-30)
Priya Singh - provide sample production traces and 95th pct latency targets (Due: 2025-09-29)
summary: Discovery focused on pilot scoping for a staged rollout: Ventana needs a hosted pilot with option to move to Dedicated or Private depending on unit economics. Main concerns: per-token unit cost, batching/caching levers, KV cache hit rates, and VPC/KMS for later phases.
transcript:
Meeting Header: 2025-09-26 15:00 UTC | Duration ~52 mins | Attendees listed above

[00:00:02] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for taking the time, um we'll kick off — quick intros, then Samira will walk through how we measure unit costs.
[00:00:12] Marco (Ventana CTO): Hi all, Marco here, we're trying to validate cost per chat session for our agent product before Q4. Budget window is tight.
[00:00:20] Priya (Ventana SRE): Priya, I own infra. We'll be running initial tests in staging, want to see hosted first then decide Dedicated or Private. Need SSO and audit logs eventually.
[00:00:30] Elliot (Product PM): Elliot, curious about latency targets — 95th percentile under 400ms ideally.
[00:00:36] Samira (Redwood SE): Great. Quick agenda: pricing levers (per-token hosted vs reserved dedicated), batching strategies, KV/prefix cache impact, and pilot scope + next steps.

[00:01:05] Samira: So on per-token hosted pricing we publish model tiers — gpt-like medium, large, etc — and e.g. approx $0.0025 per 1k input tokens and $0.03 per 1k output tokens for a large open model (note: illustrative). But the real lever is effective tokens per user session and cache hit.
[00:01:25] Marco: When you say cache hit, are we talking prefix cache for system prompts, or KV cache between turns?
[00:01:30] Samira: Both. Prefix caching takes out repeated system context, KV cache is for conversational state. Typical pilot workloads — we've seen 45-70% token reductions with KV cache when session patterns have repetition. That's huge for cost.
[00:01:48] Priya: Is KV cache something on the client or server? How does it affect latency?
[00:01:52] Samira: It's on the server runtime. We keep the KV state in memory per model shard. Cold starts cost more, but warm sessions are fast. We can set TTLs and shard affinity. Latency impact is negligible for cache hits — usually improves p95 because fewer tokens generated.

[00:02:25] Marco: Okay, so rough math: if we have 10k daily sessions with 200 tokens output median, that’s X. Can you walk through a provisioning example?
[00:02:33] Alex: Sure, two ways: hosted pay-as-you-go — you just pay per token and we auto-scale. Dedicated reserved capacity — you commit to GPU pool, lower per-token inference cost but monthly commit. For your volume, a 3-month pilot on hosted then evaluate commit makes sense.
[00:02:50] Elliot: What's the delta in unit cost between hosted and reserved?
[00:02:55] Samira: Ballpark: hosted might be 1.2–1.6x the unit cost versus a reserved worker optimized with quantization (4-bit) and tuned kernels. But the real savings come from batching and caching. For example 8-bit quant + batching could cut token compute by ~30%.

[00:03:22] Priya: Do you do model quantization ourselves or do we need a special model build?
[00:03:27] Samira: We support hosted quantized variants and also let customers bring models. For private installs we ship toolchain and suggestions — some model artifacts can be 4-bit post-training quantized. Expect some quality tradeoffs, but we run evals.

[00:03:50] Marco: Security — if we move to Dedicated or Private we need VPC peering, KMS integration, and SOC2 type II. Are those available?
[00:03:58] Alex: Yes — Dedicated includes VPC connectors and KMS/HSM integration. Private has full control plane in your VPC or on-prem. We can share SOC2 + ISO docs.

[00:04:18] Elliot: For pilot acceptance, what metrics should we capture? Latency p95, cost per session, cache hit rate?
[00:04:24] Samira: Exactly. We'll propose a benchmark plan: synth load mirroring your traces, measure p50/p90/p95, token burn, tokens per session, and cache hit. We'll also look at tail latencies when we force cache misses to understand worst-case SLA.

[00:05:02] Marco: We have a hard budget of $40k/month for the pilot. Can we scope a pilot within that?
[00:05:07] Alex: Yes, we can design a staged pilot. Initial 4-week smoke test on hosted ~estimate $8–12k depending on load. Full 8-week staging with benchmarks and two model variants could be $25–35k. If you need strict monthly cap, we can set rate limits and token quotas for the pilot.

[00:05:35] Priya: Rate limits — can you throttle by route or API key?
[00:05:39] Samira: By API key, route, and token bucket. We also provide per-token budgeting at org and project level in Console.

[00:06:02] Elliot: Explain batching — does Redwood batch across tenants? What about latency tradeoffs?
[00:06:08] Samira: We batch at the worker level. Hosted tenants are isolated by worker pool so multi-tenant batching happens only when policies allow. We favor continuous batching to keep latency low — small micro-batches every few ms. You can set max batching latency; if you need sub-200ms p95 we reduce batch windows which increases compute cost.

[00:06:38] Marco: Any guardrails for tail spikes? We can't have runaway bill on demo day.
[00:06:42] Alex: We provide budget alerts, hard caps, and automatic fallback policies — e.g., switch to a small cheaper model or degrade output quality during spikes. For Dedicated you can reserve burst nodes.

[00:07:05] Priya: On the billing side: is there line-iteming per model/inference type? We need visibility for finance.
[00:07:10] Alex: Console provides token-level breakdowns: per-model, per-route, per-key. We can export CSVs and hook to your billing system.

[00:07:30] Samira: Two important levers we'll tune during pilot: batching window and prefix KV caching policy. Example: if your sessions reuse a 512-token policy prompt, prefix cache reduces regen tokens substantially. Also caching TTL that balances freshness vs hit-rate.

[00:07:55] Marco: Real numbers — you mentioned 45–70% token reduction earlier. What assumptions there?
[00:07:59] Samira: That's in-chatbot patterns where user prompts are short and the model holds state. Where every new response reuses a 300–600 token context, KV cache prevents re-encoding those tokens. If your users include long unique documents every time, hit-rate drops. We'll baseline using your traces.

[00:08:25] Elliot: For the pilot, we want two goals: confirm p95 under 400ms at production-like qps, and confirm cost per active user under $0.05 per session. Can Redwood show a prediction?
[00:08:35] Samira: We'll run a forecast: using your sample logs, apply hit-rate assumptions (we'll do conservative 40% and optimistic 65%), and produce cost per session. That's part of the benchmark plan Samira will send.

[00:08:55] Marco: If we hit success, timeline to move to Dedicated?
[00:08:59] Alex: Dedicated provisioning is typically 2–4 weeks depending on region and GPU availability; Private longer. For Dedicated we can do canary cutover and traffic split.

[00:09:15] Priya: What's included in Dedicated SLA?
[00:09:18] Alex: Uptime SLA, latency SLOs per model class, and incident support with escalation. We'll share SLA doc.

[00:09:28] Marco: Do you support on-prem with air-gapped? We have regulatory constraints in some accounts.
[00:09:33] Alex: Yes, Private can be packaged for air-gapped environments; it's a longer engagement with professional services.

[00:09:45] (15 min marker captured in transcript noise)

[00:09:50] Samira: Let's drill into the math quickly. If we assume 10k daily sessions, median output tokens 200, that's 2M output tokens/day, ~60M tokens/month. At hosted price of $0.03 per 1k output tokens that’s about $1.8k/month raw output cost — but this is simplistic because input tokens, prompt tokens, and model overhead add up. With caching saving 50% you cut that in half. But real total includes request overhead and non-batched CPU time.
[00:10:20] Marco: Are there fixed overheads per request that affect cost even with batching?
[00:10:24] Samira: Yes: network, scheduling, and model kernel launch (if cold). We amortize that with persistent workers and batching. Cold-starts are the enemy of cost predictability.

[00:10:40] Elliot: Do you offer any tooling to simulate different batching windows and see cost/latency tradeoffs?
[00:10:44] Samira: We have an Optimize module that can run sims based on traces and recommend batch window, cache TTL, quantization, and suggest when to move to Dedicated. We'll run that for the pilot traces.

[00:11:05] Priya: For the benchmark, can Redwood run a controlled test in our staging VPC?
[00:11:09] Alex: For hosted we can spin up a staging project with IP allowlists and shared auth. For Dedicated we can do staged traffic to your reserved pool. We'll need sample traces and an allowlist.

[00:11:24] Marco: What telemetry do we get during tests?
[00:11:27] Samira: Token-level breakdown, p50/p90/p95 latency, cache hit rates, GPU utilization, batch sizes distribution. We'll provide dashboards and raw CSVs.

[00:11:40] (Small overlap) Marco: Any gotchas with model variants? We sometimes test two different open models.
[00:11:44] Samira: Different models have different compute per token. We'll include model-specific profiles in the pricing matrix. Some models are more batching-friendly.

[00:12:05] Elliot: On success criteria — acceptance for us is cost under $0.05 per session and p95 < 400ms for 80% of traffic. We can try pilot and see.

[00:12:15] Priya: Who's the primary technical contact?
[00:12:18] Marco: Priya will take lead from our side.

[00:12:22] Alex: Great. Action items recapped in the notes. We'll send a pilot SOW with pricing options: hosted-only pilot, hosted->dedicated pilot with reserved nodes, and an accelerated private eval.

[00:12:36] Samira: Also note competitors: if you trial Anthropic or OpenAI there's slightly different cost curves; we'll include an apples-to-apples comparison table.

[00:12:45] Elliot: How do we handle data retention and logs? We need 7 years for audit on some contracts — kidding — but at least audit logs and export.
[00:12:52] Alex: Console supports long-term log retention as an add-on. We can export audit logs to your SIEM.

[00:13:05] Marco: Anything else on pricing — e.g., volume discounts or overage rates?
[00:13:10] Alex: Yes volume tiers and committed commits reduce per-token. We'll include a committed capacity price deck. Also for Dedicated, commit terms (monthly/annual) change unit rate.

[00:13:25] Priya: For pilot IP allowlist and keys, who should we send to?
[00:13:29] Alex: Send to alex@redwood.example and samira@redwood.example; we'll provision a staging project.

[00:13:38] (crosstalk)

[00:13:45] Samira: I'll draft a benchmark plan that includes: ingest your traces, simulate 2 model variants, measure p95 at target qps, and iterate caching TTLs until cost/per-session target is met or we identify the blockers.

[00:14:05] Marco: Sounds good. Quick question: can you enforce hard budget caps that will stop the endpoint when threshold hit?
[00:14:10] Alex: Yes, hard caps are supported in Console and via API. We can set per-project monthly caps for the pilot.

[00:14:22] Elliot: Timeline: we want pilot kickoff next week if possible.
[00:14:26] Alex: We can aim to start smoke tests within 7 business days pending traces and allowlist.

[00:14:32] Priya: I'll get the traces over by Monday.

[00:14:35] Alex: Great — again we'll produce a pricing matrix, pilot SOW, and proposed benchmark plan. Any final Qs?

[00:14:45] Marco: No, thanks. Appreciate the clarity on caching and batching.
[00:14:50] Elliot: Thanks all.

[00:14:55] Alex: We'll follow up with docs. Meeting adjourned.

[00:15:00] (call ended)

Note: transcript contains casual speech, occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., "K-V cache" vs KV, "SageMaker" sometimes transcribed as "Sage Maker").
